The elemental sulfur recovered in the gasification process can also be disposed of by burial, with little or no contamination resulting.
In the coal gasification scenario, there would be an adverse and unavoidable impact on the water quality of streams crossed by the water supply and delivery pipelines. During construction and for a period afterwards the rate of sediment erosion by water and wind would be increased along the right-of-ways. In stream crossing areas, lateral scour and channel scour would be increased. Such effects can be lessened through proper construction practices and placement of protective rip-rap or sandbags, where necessary. Erosion rates along the right-of-ways would be considerably greater than adjacent areas for at least a year following construction. Locally, severe erosion could result in gullying of slopes, and possibly exposing or undermining the pipeline. Erosion can be minimized by revegetating disturbed areas and through a variety of construction measures within the trenches.
The main degradation of water quality would be due to an increased sediment load and to a minor extent through increases in dissolved solids. Project-related sediment load should decrease abruptly following construction and gradually thereafter until within a few years it probably will not be detectably different from preconstruction levels.
Water quality could be degraded through accidental spills of fuels, oils, herbicides, chemicals, or other solids or liquids used during construction or maintenance of the pipeline.
